brief.head: Friends by choice
brief.text: The in­ter­net let Amit Varma’s “cusp gen­er­a­tion” move from com­mu­ni­ties of cir­cum­stance to com­mu­ni­ties of choice[[x3]][[x4]], he said. Almost all his close friends now come from the lat­ter. {126-C01}

brief.head: Body and mind apart
brief.text: In women, phys­i­cal and psy­cho­log­i­cal arousal are sep­a­rate pro­cesses, Amit Varma said. So a body’s re­sponse dur­ing rape is not con­sent, nor se­cret en­joy­ment. {126-C12}

brief.head: Clever, for her sake
brief.text: Where fe­males are choosy, males must com­pete. “In hu­mans, men are smart be­cause women are se­lec­tive,” Amit Varma said; Steven Pinker sug­gests art may be male or­na­men­ta­tion. {126-C17}

brief.head: Green-eyed, two ways
brief.text: Male jeal­ousy is sex­ual, fe­male jeal­ousy emo­tional, Amit Varma said. With con­di­tion­ing and pa­tri­archy, he thinks this partly ex­plains why wives for­give in­fi­delity more often than hus­bands. {126-C16}

lead.kicker: Amit Varma reads the evolutionary science of desire
lead.head: He wants pictures, she wants plots

pic.caption: Ajay Shah (left) and Amit Varma early in Episode 126

body: Amit Varma had al­ready given this talk once, at a Goa meetup of Life Lessons, the on­line course he runs with Ajay Shah. He warned the room that it was “not a prac­ti­cal class, but the­ory, the­ory.” {126-J01}

In Episode 126 of *Everything is Everything*, he gave it again for Shah: the what and the why of human sex­u­al­ity, drawn largely from one book, *A Billion Wicked Thoughts* by Ogi Ogas and Say Gaddam.

Where Alfred Kinsey asked peo­ple what they did, the book looks at what they do on­line: what men and women search for[[x1]], and what ro­mance nov­els sell. “Scientists have an eas­ier time gaz­ing at in­ter­ga­lac­tic quasars than peek­ing into someone’s bed­room,” its au­thors write.
## Two dif­fer­ent bets

The root, Varma said, lies in hunter-gatherer times. Spreading his genes cost a man noth­ing. A woman paid with nine months of preg­nancy and years of child-rearing, and got only a few shots. {126-C06}
So men are wired to seek quan­tity and women to be se­lec­tive, choos­ing both good genes and a re­li­able provider. From this, Varma said, flows nearly every dif­fer­ence be­tween the sexes.
He in­sisted it was “a de­scrip­tion, not a pre­scrip­tion”.
The book’s head­line find­ing fol­lows, as Varma put it: “men are into vis­ual cues and im­ages, women are into sto­ries and nar­ra­tives.”
## Clips and pa­per­backs
The ev­i­dence is in be­hav­iour. When the book was writ­ten, Varma said, about 2 per cent of credit-card pay­ments for porn came from women. About 90 per cent of ro­mance nov­els are read by women.
Ogas and Gaddam put the con­trast starkly. A 60-second clip can be enough for a man, but the most pop­u­lar aid to women’s arousal is a 250-page book “that re­quires hours to di­gest”. {126-C10}
In women’s minds, the au­thors say, runs “Miss Marple’s de­tec­tive agency”: so­cial, cul­tural, emo­tional and phys­i­cal de­tec­tives vet­ting every suitor. Men have only the phys­i­cal one.

Hence what they call the power of or and the power of and. One cue can be enough for a man. For a woman, looks, con­ver­sa­tion, at­ten­tion and sta­tus must all line up. “Is he a chauf­feur or is he a CEO?” Varma asked. {126-C13}
Romance nov­els, Varma said, re­veal women’s pref­er­ences as porn re­veals men’s. Their he­roes are dom­i­nant, rich and, in the end, tamed.
## Agency, not des­tiny

Why study any of this? Understanding human na­ture, Varma said, “in­creases both our agency and our com­pas­sion”. Both hosts, he noted, are hard­wired to want chil­dren, and both chose not to have any.
He asked lis­ten­ers not to leap from what is nat­u­ral to what is right, and Shah re­minded them that an av­er­age is not an iden­tity.

Varma closed with Madame de Staël, whose line he thinks lies at the heart of human sex­u­al­ity: “The de­sire of the man is for the woman. The de­sire of the woman is for the de­sire of the man.” {126-C20}

Shah had the last se­ri­ous word. Traditional so­ci­ety wrapped sex­u­al­ity in in­hi­bi­tion, he said, and mod­ern so­cial media cul­ture en­forces “very old fash­ioned norms”, in many pe­cu­liar ways more tox­i­cally.
He urged read­ers to read the book all the same. “A lot of it is un­com­fort­able,” he said.

second.label: Intelligence
second.head: Licence to remember
second.deck: Ajay Shah says women who helped hunt bin Laden hold a lesson for India

pic.caption: Ajay Shah on the women who hunted bin Laden

body: Intelligence op­er­a­tives, in our men­tal model, are men out of a John le Carré book or a James Bond movie, Ajay Shah said. Yet the traits Amit Varma had just de­scribed in women would work ex­tremely well in the field.

Varma had ar­gued that women tend to have bet­ter mem­o­ries and a sharper eye for de­tail. In the CIA’s hunt for Osama bin Laden, Shah said, crit­i­cal per­sons were women, able to hold vast data­bases in their heads and spot what fell out of pat­tern. {126-S04}
India, he said, should re­build its in­tel­li­gence forces with many, many women hires. It sounded glib, Varma said, but both of them meant it se­ri­ously. {#glib}

quote.text: They had that abil­ity to hold vast data­bases in their head and see one thing fall­ing out of pat­tern.

third.head: Fowl play in the barnyard

pic.caption: Amit Varma on the roosters and the feathered board

body: Sometimes, Amit Varma said, vis­ual cues mat­ter so much that the woman doesn’t mat­ter at all. He read from *A Billion Wicked Thoughts* on bi­ol­o­gists test­ing which cues set off mat­ing be­hav­iour in male fowl. {126-C09}

“About half of all roost­ers at­tempted cop­u­la­tion with an ar­ti­fi­cial chicken head mounted on a feather cov­ered board.” Turkeys were less dis­crim­i­nat­ing still: male gob­blers will try to mate with a rub­ber ball of the size and height of a fe­male head.
Varma saw the same logic in hen­tai, a kind of anime in which every cue is ex­ag­ger­ated. {#hentai}

Ajay Shah of­fered an anal­ogy: porn thrived when screens were 640 by 480 pix­els, and was “al­ways the pi­o­neer­ing app that drove com­puter usage”. Varma re­called dial-up days, wait­ing for a pic­ture of Samantha Fox[[x2]] to load. {126-J07}

box.title: A book of revealed desires
box.text: *A Billion Wicked Thoughts*, by Ogi Ogas and Say Gaddam, stud­ies what peo­ple search for[[x6]] and read on­line, not what they tell re­searchers. Amit Varma read a phys­i­cal copy, un­der­lined nearly every page, and said it made what he knew in­tu­itively “high def­i­ni­tion”. {126-R01}

sections.label: The what and why
sections.head: From questionnaires to clicks
sections.caption: the what and the why of sexuality
body: To un­der­stand sex­u­al­ity, Amit Varma said, we need two things: what we are, and why we are that way. Neither is well un­der­stood. “We know very lit­tle about our own sex­ual de­sires, we are in de­nial of a lot of them.”

The what began with Alfred Kinsey, who, Varma said, put 521 ques­tions to many thou­sands of re­spon­dents. {#kinsey521} His books on men and women over­turned myths about ho­mo­sex­u­al­ity and fe­male plea­sure.
But his re­spon­dents came from elite Westernised so­ci­ety, and they were stat­ing their pref­er­ences. {#elite}
## The why

The why came from evo­lu­tion. After Richard Dawkins’s *The Selfish Gene* in 1975, Varma said, the next big mile­stone was Donald Symons’s *The Evolution of Human Sexuality* in 1979, which used nat­u­ral se­lec­tion to ex­plain why men and women are wired dif­fer­ently. {126-R05}

Varma also read Steven Pinker’s *The Blank Slate* and books that built on Symons: Geoffrey Miller’s *The Mating Mind*, David Buss’s *The Evolution of Desire*, Robert Wright’s *The Moral Animal*. None of them, he said, treats na­ture and nur­ture as a bi­nary. {126-C21}

*A Billion Wicked Thoughts* joins the strands. It stud­ies anonymised on­line be­hav­iour, from porn searches to ro­mance read­er­ship, and ex­plains it with nat­u­ral se­lec­tion, psy­chol­ogy and so­ci­ol­ogy.
~ Varma called this a book episode, in the line of ear­lier ones on Henry Hazlitt’s *Economics in One Lesson* and James C. Scott’s *Seeing Like a State*.

quote.text: he was right so triv­ially that today it bog­gles the mind that he was treated the way he was.

sections.label: Four reasons
sections.head: Know thyself, then others
sections.caption: why sexuality is worth knowing
body: People often talk about sex al­most guiltily, Amit Varma said, but it is core to un­der­stand­ing our­selves. He gave four rea­sons to study it.

The first is the in­scrip­tion at the Temple of Apollo at Delphi[[x7]]: know thy­self[[x8]]. {126-J15} Otherwise, he said, we gaslight our­selves about our urges. Before we can be kind to oth­ers, we must be kind to our­selves; be­fore that, we must know our­selves.

The sec­ond is to know oth­ers, in­stead of judg­ing them by our own in­stincts. He quoted Donald Symons: “To en­counter erot­ica de­signed to ap­peal to the other sex is to gaze into the psy­cho­log­i­cal abyss that sep­a­rates the sexes.” {126-J16}
## Agency and mis­match
Third, know­ing our wiring lets us over­ride it. Everyone is hard­wired to have kids, Varma said; he and Ajay Shah de­cided not to have any. {126-C02}

Fourth, our in­stincts were built for hunter-gatherer times and are mis­matched with the mod­ern world. Ogas and Gaddam write that “porn, dat­ing apps and birth con­trol hi­jack an­cient cir­cuits meant for scarcity and re­pro­duc­tion.” {#hijack}
~ Varma ad­mit­ted to vi­o­lent in­stincts of his own, which he has learned not to act on. He is, he said, “fully Bengali, but in traf­fic I be­come a Punjabi.”

quote.text: I be­lieve un­der­stand­ing human na­ture in­creases both our agency and our com­pas­sion.

sections.label: Four caveats
sections.head: Ought, is and the rasgulla
sections.caption: reading nature without misreading it
body: Amit Varma said he was ter­ri­fied that clips from the episode would cir­cu­late with­out con­text, so he began with four caveats. {#clips}

First, the is-ought prob­lem[[x10]], which he at­trib­uted to David Hume. If men are wired to be pro­mis­cu­ous, it does not fol­low that they should be. We are hard­wired for vi­o­lence too. “You do not get to an ought from an is.” {126-C03}

Second, the nat­u­ral­is­tic fal­lacy, a term he cred­ited to G. E. Moore, around 1903: treat­ing nat­u­ral as good. Bigots once called ho­mo­sex­u­al­ity un­nat­u­ral and there­fore bad. It is per­fectly nat­u­ral in our species and many oth­ers, Varma said, and the ar­gu­ment would be a fal­lacy even if it were not.
## Proximate and ul­ti­mate

Third, do not con­fuse prox­i­mate causes with ul­ti­mate ones[[x9]]. We like sweets be­cause, when calo­ries were un­pre­dictable, those who stocked up sur­vived. {126-C04} But Ajay Shah, Varma said, “likes a ras­gulla today be­cause he just does.”

Fourth, every gen­er­al­i­sa­tion has ex­cep­tions. Shah made the point with shoe sizes: on av­er­age older chil­dren have big­ger feet, yet five-year-olds vary enor­mously among them­selves. {#shoesize}
~ Varma had joked on the course’s WhatsApp group that mem­bers read a paper a day on av­er­age: 139 read none and Shah reads 140 a night. Shah said he av­er­ages three a week. {126-J02}

quote.text: So on av­er­age, some­thing can be true, but that’s not our es­sen­tial iden­tity.

sections.label: The root of it
sections.head: Sow widely, choose wisely
sections.caption: promiscuous men and selective women
body: Before turn­ing to the book, Amit Varma set out what the field al­ready agrees on. Its first two points go to­gether: men are wired to be pro­mis­cu­ous, women to be se­lec­tive. {126-C06}

In hunter-gatherer times, he said, a man’s in­cen­tive was to spread his genes as widely as pos­si­ble, “and there is no cost to spread­ing his genes. Not for him.” A woman faced preg­nancy and years of rais­ing a baby, with no pill and no rhythm method.
So women se­lect in two ways, Varma said: for men whose genes are likely to spread, and for a man who will look after mother and child. These are often two dif­fer­ent men.
## Youth, sta­tus, ro­mance

From the asym­me­try, he ar­gued, comes the next pair. Men are drawn to youth and beauty[[x11]], signs of present and fu­ture fer­til­ity. Women are drawn to sta­tus and power, to the chief of the tribe.

Romance and jeal­ousy are adap­ta­tions too, keep­ing a fam­ily to­gether around the child. Robert Wright’s *The Moral Animal*, Varma said, shows how such im­pulses can set­tle into monogamy or polygamy, de­pend­ing on a society’s di­rec­tion. {#wright}
~ None of this is a value judge­ment, he stressed. “It’s not jus­ti­fi­ca­tion. It’s just ex­pla­na­tion.”

quote.text: Men are wired to be pro­mis­cu­ous, women are wired to be se­lec­tive.

sections.label: Men and images
sections.head: What the search bar knows
sections.caption: men’s searches and fertility cues
body: Men pre­fer vis­ual cues, Amit Varma said, and what they look for are signs of youth and fer­til­ity. Porn searches re­veal what men like[[x12]], not what they say they like.

Ornaments such as the peacock’s tail at­tract mates even when they at­tract preda­tors. In hu­mans, beauty sig­nals health: ideal fe­male faces dif­fer across cul­tures, but all are sym­met­ri­cal. “We find sym­me­try beau­ti­ful be­cause it is a sign of good health.” {126-C07}
Searches for “fat” or “over­weight” out­num­ber those for “skinny” three to one. {#fat} The skinny ideal, Ogas and Gaddam sug­gest, comes from women’s mag­a­zines such as *Vogue* and *Cosmopolitan*.
Men pre­fer a waist-to-hip ratio of 0.7 with­out ever search­ing for hips. In an English bar, a woman was hit on far more often as pad­ding took her from an A cup to a C cup. {#acup}
## The small-feet puz­zle

Varma had long won­dered why feet are erotic in al­most every cul­ture. The an­swer: healthy oe­stro­gen lev­els pro­duce gy­noid fat in breasts and but­tocks, and small feet, so the three go to­gether. {#gynoid}
Nobody thinks about oe­stro­gen, he said: “we are just drawn to these areas of the human body with­out ever ac­tu­ally know­ing why.” {126-C08}
~ Varma, who says he is not drawn to small feet him­self, counts as one of the ex­cep­tions.

quote.text: our in­stincts are hard­wired in such a way that we are drawn to these signs of fer­til­ity

sections.label: Women and stories
sections.head: Taming the wild coconut
sections.caption: romance as the porn for women
body: “Romance is to women what porn is to men,” Amit Varma said. Romance is the largest genre in fic­tion by far, and about 90 per cent of ro­mance nov­els are read by women. {#ninety}

He quizzed Ajay Shah on *The Flame and the Flower*, which he called the first ro­mance novel pub­lished straight to pa­per­back, after which the genre took off. Shah, in the post-lunch blues, did not guess.

The nov­els re­veal women’s pref­er­ences as porn re­veals men’s, Varma said. Heroes are dom­i­nant, and the cen­tral fan­tasy is tam­ing the wild co­conut. “A co­conut is some­thing that is hard on the out­side and soft on the in­side.” {#coconut}
Status mat­ters too. Ogas and Gaddam counted 415 mil­lion­aires, 286 bil­lion­aires and 263 sheikhs in ro­mance ti­tles on Amazon. {126-C14}
## Two delu­sions

Each sex, Varma said, has its great self-delusion. For women, it is find­ing the ex­cit­ing bad boy and the steady provider in one man. For men, it is that they can re­li­ably sat­isfy a woman. {126-C15}
~ Seldom, he said, can any­one com­bine “the sex­ual al­lure of the younger Ajay Shah and the re­spon­si­ble vibe of the older Ajay Shah”. {126-J11}

quote.text: the great self delu­sion for women is that they can get both the men in one body.

Sometimes nur­ture am­pli­fies na­ture, some­times it mit­i­gates na­ture, which is to my mind the project of civil­i­sa­tion, to mit­i­gate the worst in­stincts of our hard wiring and choose who we want to be and live ac­cord­ingly.

p3.title: Pillow talk
p3.deck: A martyr of sex research, a blogger’s finest hour, and other tales

stories.kicker: Amit Varma on the man who asked America about sex
stories.head: Right too soon, and paid for it
body: In the mid­dle of the twen­ti­eth cen­tury, a re­searcher called Alfred Kinsey set out to dis­cover what human sex­u­al­ity is: what urges peo­ple have and how they be­have. He put, Amit Varma said, 521 ques­tions to many thou­sands of re­spon­dents.

The re­sults busted myths. People be­lieved ho­mo­sex­u­al­ity was fringe, de­viant be­hav­iour prac­tised by very few. His sur­vey found that as many as a third of men ad­mit­ted to a ho­mo­sex­ual ex­pe­ri­ence. {#third}

The no­tion that women did not re­ally feel sex­ual plea­sure fell too. A sig­nif­i­cant chunk of women, Varma said, mas­tur­bated, thought about sex and slept with men other than their hus­bands. “That’s awe­some. It’s a cel­e­bra­tion of sex­u­al­ity.”

The find­ings on women were not palat­able to so­ci­ety, even in America. The vol­ume on men ap­peared in 1948 and the one on women in 1953, at which point the Rockefeller Foundation dropped his fund­ing[[x13]]. {#rockefeller} Varma thought he could no longer teach at his uni­ver­sity ei­ther, though he did not re­mem­ber the de­tails.
Kinsey died at 62, of pneu­mo­nia. {#sixtytwo} “But I have no doubt that there was a lot of pain for him in his last years be­cause no one took his work se­ri­ously,” Varma said.

Kinsey had his lim­its, Varma al­lowed: his re­spon­dents were elite and Westernised, and stated their pref­er­ences rather than re­veal­ing them. Yet he was right, Varma said, so ob­vi­ously that his treat­ment now bog­gles the mind. {126-S02}

~ Varma likened him to Ignaz Semmelweis, who first ex­posed the im­por­tance of hand-washing be­fore surgery. No one took him se­ri­ously, peo­ple kept dying, and Semmelweis died in a lu­natic asy­lum. {#semmelweis}
stories.why: Those who re­port un­com­fort­able truths are often pun­ished in their life­times and vin­di­cated so com­pletely af­ter­wards that their treat­ment looks ab­surd. What one gen­er­a­tion finds un­speak­able, a later one may find ob­vi­ous.

pic.caption: Amit Varma on Alfred Kinsey’s fate

stories.kicker: Amit Varma recalls his blogging days
stories.head: Bhabhi bookmarks India Uncut
body: Ajay Shah in­tro­duced it as “one of the high­lights of Amit Varma’s life”. Around 2006 or 2007, an adult comic called *Savita Bhabhi* was be­com­ing pop­u­lar; its hero­ine had wild ad­ven­tures with vis­it­ing plumbers and ladies’ tai­lors.
Varma was then run­ning India Uncut, a hugely pop­u­lar blog[[x14]]: some 8,000 posts in five years, about five a day. {#posts}
~ He wrote about the comic, and likes to think he was one of the rea­sons it ex­ploded and went viral, in the days be­fore Twitter. {#viral}
Then one day he opened the lat­est edi­tion to find its hero­ine dis­cussing her favourite blog. It was India Uncut. “So what greater achieve­ment could there be, Ajay Shah?” he asked. {126-S03}
stories.why: Before Twitter, vi­ral­ity ran through blogs, and a pop­u­lar blog­ger could lift an un­der­ground comic as surely as the comic could re­turn the favour. Varma tells it with self-mocking pride.
stories.postscript: Varma also wrote a naughty ver­sion of *My Bonnie Lies Over the Ocean* for the Bengali boudi: “My Boudi Lies Over the Lotion.” {126-J06}

pic.caption: Amit Varma (right) on Savita Bhabhi’s favourite blog, with Ajay Shah

stories.kicker: What the body knows before the mind does
stories.head: A monthly tipping point
body: Just be­fore his talk at the Goa meetup, Amit Varma promised a group of women: “Ladies, I’m gonna go up there and I’m gonna mansplain to you about ovu­la­tion.” {126-J09}

The find­ing: ovu­lat­ing women, whether they know it or not, tend to dress more re­veal­ingly and be more open to bad-boy types. Among lap dancers, the ovu­lat­ing earned by far the high­est tips and the men­stru­at­ing the least. {#tips} Whether the dancers be­haved dif­fer­ently or the men sensed some­thing, no­body knows.

Most strik­ing to Varma, men grew more pro­tec­tive of their part­ners dur­ing ovu­la­tion, though they have no way of know­ing it. “There is some­thing hap­pen­ing at a sub­lim­i­nal in­stinc­tive level which we are not even aware of,” he said. {126-S05}
~ In a blind smell test, women found the most dom­i­nant, high-status men the sex­i­est by body odour. {#smell}
stories.why: Much mat­ing be­hav­iour, Varma sug­gested, runs on sig­nals that nei­ther sender nor re­ceiver con­sciously per­ceives. The body keeps its own cal­en­dar be­neath aware­ness, which is one more rea­son, in his telling, to study our wiring rather than deny it.

pic.caption: Amit Varma on ovulation and the lap dancers

stories.kicker: Amit Varma and Ajay Shah on their Life Lessons meetup
stories.head: Fifty came, seven on sabbatical
body: After three co­horts of their course Life Lessons in 2025, with some 130 par­tic­i­pants, Amit Varma and Ajay Shah planned a meetup in Goa and hoped for 20 or 30 peo­ple. Between 50 and 60 came, book­ing their own flights and ho­tels. {#fiftysixty}

At the first lunch, the first seven peo­ple to join Varma were all on sab­bat­i­cal. {#sabbatical} He cred­its a se­lec­tion ef­fect: a pre­mium price and se­ri­ous con­tent drew cu­ri­ous peo­ple with agency.
Varma calls him­self a so­cially awk­ward in­tro­vert whom large crowds make un­com­fort­able. Yet in Goa he felt at ease with ev­ery­one. {126-S01}

~ Last-minute sign-ups ar­rived, Shah said, one from Thailand and one from New York. {#thailand} Varma blamed the FOMO in the course’s WhatsApp group, and re­called singing, danc­ing and a man with a ukulele.

quote.text: this was the only gath­er­ing in my life where I just felt im­me­di­ately at ease and com­fort­able with each and every per­son.

quiz.q: How many questions did Alfred Kinsey put to his respondents, by Amit Varma’s account?
quiz.a: Five hun­dred and twenty-one, to many thou­sands of peo­ple in elite Westernised so­ci­ety.

quiz.q: Which blog did the heroine of the comic *Savita Bhabhi* name as her favourite?
quiz.a: India Uncut, Amit Varma’s own blog, which ran some 8,000 posts in five years.

quiz.q: What do Ogas and Gaddam call the set of four detectives in women’s minds?
quiz.a: Miss Marple’s Detective Agency: so­cial, cul­tural, emo­tional and phys­i­cal de­tec­tives vet­ting po­ten­tial mates.

quiz.q: Why, according to Amit Varma, is it far harder to turn on a woman than a man?
quiz.a: Male arousal runs on the power of or; fe­male arousal needs the power of and.

quiz.q: What did Ajay Shah’s shoe-size example teach about generalisations concerning men and women?
quiz.a: Something can be true on av­er­age with­out being anyone’s es­sen­tial iden­tity.

quiz.q: Whose line did Varma close with, about the desire of the man and of the woman?
quiz.a: Madame de Staël’s: the woman’s de­sire is for the de­sire of the man.

p4.credits: Everything is Everything was Amit Varma and Ajay Shah’s weekly show, 128 episodes from June 2023 to December 2025. This edition is made from Episode 126. The moving pictures, stills and chapter cards are from its video; the chapter art is by Simahina. Every play button starts the video at the moment it was said. The articles and headlines were written by Claude, an AI model, from the episode’s machine-made transcript, and checked against it. Other photographs are from Wikimedia Commons: Alfred Kinsey (Wikimedia Commons, public domain); Richard Dawkins (David Shankbone, CC BY 3.0); David Hume (Allan Ramsay, public domain); G. E. Moore (Wikimedia Commons, public domain); Steven Pinker (Christopher Michel, CC BY-SA 4.0). The covers on the shelf are from Amazon.

shelf.title: A Billion Wicked Thoughts
shelf.creator: Ogi Ogas and Say Gaddam
shelf.why: Uses hard data on anonymised in­ter­net be­hav­iour, re­vealed rather than stated pref­er­ences, to show what men and women want, and ex­plains why through nat­u­ral se­lec­tion.

shelf.title: Sexual Behavior in the Human Male
shelf.creator: Alfred Kinsey & others
shelf.why: It blew apart myths of its time, for in­stance show­ing that about a third of men ad­mit­ted a ho­mo­sex­ual ex­pe­ri­ence.

shelf.title: Sexual Behavior in the Human Female
shelf.creator: Alfred Kinsey & others
shelf.why: It showed that women have rich sex­ual lives (mas­tur­ba­tion, fan­tasy, part­ners be­yond their hus­bands), over­turn­ing the be­lief that sex­u­al­ity was mainly a male thing.

shelf.title: The Selfish Gene
shelf.creator: Richard Dawkins
shelf.why: Dawkins’s metaphor of the self­ish gene which, read care­fully rather than lit­er­ally, ex­plains why hu­mans are ca­pa­ble of love and al­tru­ism.

shelf.title: The Evolution of Human Sexuality
shelf.creator: Donald Symons
shelf.why: Symons used nat­u­ral se­lec­tion to ex­plain why men and women are wired dif­fer­ently: a for­ma­tive book for Amit that set off a flood of later work, its ar­gu­ments later con­firmed with data by A Billion Wicked Thoughts.

shelf.title: The Blank Slate
shelf.creator: Steven Pinker
shelf.why: Amit’s gate­way into nat­u­ral se­lec­tion and evo­lu­tion­ary psy­chol­ogy: Pinker ex­am­ines human na­ture and so­ci­ety through our evo­lu­tion­ary hard­wiring.

shelf.title: The Mating Mind
shelf.creator: Geoffrey Miller
shelf.why: Part of the group of books that showed him how bi­ol­ogy works on human de­sire, and on his read­ing list for this sub­ject.

shelf.title: The Evolution of Desire
shelf.creator: David Buss
shelf.why: It builds the evo­lu­tion­ary ac­count of why men and women want what they want, which forms the shared ground this episode starts from.

shelf.title: The Moral Animal
shelf.creator: Robert Wright
shelf.why: Amit’s pick among books on nat­u­ral se­lec­tion be­cause it deals with moral­ity: how evo­lu­tion pro­duced our bet­ter in­stincts (it taught him ‘re­cip­ro­cal altruism’) and how mar­riage evolved, with monogamy and polygamy as adap­ta­tions to dif­fer­ent cir­cum­stances.

shelf.title: Warrior Lovers
shelf.creator: Catherine Salmon and Donald Symons
shelf.why: It con­trasts the male fan­tasy world of ‘pornotopia’ (lust with­out courtship) with the ro­mance novel, which it reads as a chron­i­cle of fe­male mate choice.

shelf.title: Is–Ought Problem
shelf.creator: Wikipedia
shelf.why: Hume’s point that you can­not de­rive an ‘ought’ from an ‘is’ guards against read­ing evo­lu­tion­ary ex­pla­na­tions as moral jus­ti­fi­ca­tions.

shelf.title: Life Lessons
shelf.creator: Amit Varma & Ajay Shah
shelf.why: Amit and Ajay’s course on what they wish they had been taught at twenty: learn­ing how to learn, frame­works for think­ing, writ­ing, prob­a­bilis­tic in­tu­ition, eco­nom­ics, the his­tory of thought, per­sonal fi­nance (Ajay’s mod­ule is ‘legendary’) and health.

shelf.title: Everything is Everything Ep 125: Understanding Evolution
shelf.creator: Amit Varma & Ajay Shah
shelf.why: It lays the nat­u­ral-selection ground­work that this episode’s ‘why’ of sex­u­al­ity de­pends on.

laughs.text: On pre­sent­ing the sex­u­al­ity ses­sion at Goa, Amit was ‘at pains to give the caveat to ev­ery­one present that this is not a prac­ti­cal class, but the­ory, the­ory.’

After Ajay’s les­son on av­er­ages, Amit’s WhatsApp joke: ‘On Life Lessons, ev­ery­body reads an av­er­age of one paper a day. But what’s re­ally hap­pen­ing is 139 of us don’t read pa­pers at all, and Ajay Shah reads 140 pa­pers every night.’ Ajay cor­rects him: ‘I’m av­er­ag­ing three pa­pers a week.’

Amit, trip­ping over ‘who they are, who be them’: ‘Who says who be them? Gentle read­ers, I’m sorry, we are grow­ing old. Enjoy these episodes while they last, we’ll be a bab­bling mess in a scant few weeks.’

Ajay notes that porn thrived even on weak 640x480 screens and was ‘al­ways the pi­o­neer­ing app that drove com­puter usage’. Amit re­calls dial-up days when ‘Samantha Fox is half done, she’s at the neck and you’re wait­ing for the rest to come.’

Amit’s CEO joke, from their friend Narendra Shenoy: a CEO gives each of three girl­friends a mil­lion dol­lars. One beau­ti­fies her­self, one buys him a Sony FX3 and XM4 head­phones, and one in­vests in di­ver­si­fied index funds ‘just as you rec­om­mend in our fi­nance webinar’ and turns it into three mil­lion. ‘Who does he choose? He chooses the one with the big boobs.’ Ajay: ‘I didn’t see that com­ing.’ Amit: ‘I’m glad it came.’

Amit: ‘Ajay Shah, you’re so lov­able. Is this in­ten­tional or are you just nat­u­rally a lit­tle woman?’ Ajay: ‘I’m fifty-nine years old. I grew up.’ Amit: ‘Nobody grows up... There are no adults... Adulting is the big­gest con job that they tell you.’
Ogas and Gaddam’s open­ing ob­ser­va­tion that we un­der­stand our sex­u­al­ity poorly: ‘Scientists have an eas­ier time gaz­ing at in­ter­ga­lac­tic quasars than peek­ing into someone’s bed­room.’
‘Know thyself’, the in­scrip­tion at the Temple of Apollo at Delphi, to­gether with Socrates’s ‘the un­ex­am­ined life is not worth living’, as Amit’s first rea­son for study­ing sex­u­al­ity.
Donald Symons: ‘To en­counter erot­ica de­signed to ap­peal to the other sex is to gaze into the psy­cho­log­i­cal abyss that sep­a­rates the sexes.’
